rationale: The earlier notice says Jerusalem was large but had few people; the later allocation of one in ten to live there addresses that particular population shortage.

relationship: Volunteers alongside the lot allocation; same-chapter
rationale: The blessing of those who willingly settle in Jerusalem follows the lot assigning one in ten to the city. The voluntary offers and the lottery allocation are distinct, rather than every selected resident being called a volunteer.

Both introductions describe Israel, priests, Levites and temple servants living in their possessions, then name Judah and Benjamin among Jerusalem's residents; Chronicles additionally names Ephraim and Manasseh, while Nehemiah names Salomon's slaves.

Both Jerusalem lists include the Judah line of Phares, but Nehemiah names Athaia with a longer ancestral chain and Chronicles names Gothi with a different chain. The shared family section does not identify those men as one person.

The corresponding Judah entries use Seloni and Selonites, but name Maasia and Asaia respectively and give different family detail. The similar family designation is preserved without identifying the differently named men.

Both Benjamin sections begin with Selo/Salo and Mesoulam/Mosollam, but the subsequent ancestors differ: Nehemiah continues through Joad and Phadaia, whereas Chronicles has Odouia and Sanaa. The chains are not made into one genealogy.

Nehemiah gives 928 after Gebi and Seli, while the corresponding Chronicles section gives 956 for the brethren according to their generations and names other men. The population labels and totals are compared without assuming identical enumerated groups.

Both priestly sections include Jachin and similar preceding forms, but Nehemiah says Jadia son of Jorib, while Chronicles lists Jodae and Joarim separately. The different name forms and father-son syntax remain explicit.

The Jerusalem priestly entries share a closely corresponding ancestral sequence, Elkia/Chelkia through Aitob/Achitob, but begin with Saraia and Azaria respectively. Nehemiah's opposite the house of God is not replaced by Chronicles' leader of the house of God, and the heads are not identified as one person.

Nehemiah has Samaia son of Asoub son of Ezri; Chronicles has Samaia son of Asob son of Esrikam and continues the line through Asabia to Merari. The differing forms and the extra ancestry are retained rather than silently merged.

The parallel section contains Mathania/Manthanias son of Micha and Obed/Abdia with Samoui/Samia, but Chronicles supplies additional names and ancestry. These are compared as register forms, without asserting that each differing personal form establishes the same individual.

Both gatekeeper sections name Akoub, and have Telamin/Talman, while Chronicles also names Salom and Aiman. Nehemiah's 172 total is not supplied by this target unit or substituted for the different count later in Chronicles.

The overseer comes from Asaph's singers; the later historical note expressly recalls Asaph's leading place among the singers in David's days, giving the named tradition behind the family role without identifying the overseer as Asaph himself.

Kariatharbok in the Judah settlement list can be compared with Joshua's explanation that Hebron was formerly the city of Arbok and was given to Caleb. The later settlers are not identified as the same inhabitants from Joshua's time.

The Beersabee settlement notice corresponds to Beer-sheba with its villages in Judah's inheritance list; the place-name forms are retained and no identity of the populations across periods is inferred.
Lachis with its fields in the resettlement account corresponds to Lachish among Judah's inherited towns. The comparison concerns the named locality, not the unchanged ownership of each field.

Machamas in the Benjamin settlement notice can be compared with the men of Machmas in the earlier return register; the variant place form is preserved and the later residents are not individually identified with the 122 returnees.

The list's heading places these priests and Levites with Zorobabel and Jesus on the return; Ezra's return register likewise opens with Zorobabel and Iesous among its leaders, while listing different additional names.

relationship: Named priestly families represented later; same-chapter
rationale: Saraia, Jermia and Esdra in the earlier list reappear as family labels for Maraia, Anania and Mesoulam in Joakim's days. The later representatives are distinguished from the earlier names.

relationship: Later representatives of two priestly families; same-chapter
rationale: The earlier names Amaria and Malouch recur in the family-head list associated respectively with Joanan and Jonathan; this compares the stated family sequence, not one person's names.
Sechenia in the earlier priestly list reappears as the family designation for Joseph in the later list for Joakim's days.

relationship: Priestly lists situated by generations; same-chapter
rationale: The first list is dated to the days of Jesus; the following genealogy names his son Joakim, and the later family-head list is expressly dated to Joakim's days. The lists are not treated as simultaneous.

Both Levitical lists include Jesou/Iesous and Kadmiel. Ezra gives a 74-person entry with Odouia ancestry, while this list includes additional names and duties; the Levite Jesou is not identified as the high priest Jesus merely by name.
The genealogy says Jesus fathered Joakim, and the later notice calls Joakim son of Jesus, son of Josedek, adding the prior generation without changing the stated parentage.

relationship: Later representatives recall earlier family names; same-chapter
rationale: Maraia and Anania are assigned to Saraia and Jermia, names already present in the list of priests who returned with Zorobabel and Jesus; the representatives and family names remain distinct.

relationship: Esdra and Amaria in both priestly lists; same-chapter
rationale: The earlier list names Esdra and Amaria; the later one associates Mesoulam and Joanan with those families. This does not identify the earlier Esdra with the separately mentioned priest and scribe Esdras.

relationship: Malouch and Sechenia in both lists; same-chapter
rationale: Jonathan and Joseph are assigned to Malouch and Sechenia, the two names in the earlier priestly list, preserving the difference between family labels and their later representatives.

relationship: Levitical registration and its named record; same-chapter
rationale: The statement that Levitical family heads were registered is followed by the more specific notice of their record in the book of the accounts of the days and its endpoint. The book is not identified as canonical Chronicles, and differing name forms or generations are not reconciled.

relationship: Scope of the recorded family heads; same-chapter
rationale: The book notice concerns the Levitical family heads whose registration has just been described, while the preceding verse separately mentions priests under Darius. The record's Joanan son of Elisoub wording is retained without silently inserting another generation.

Nehemiah explicitly attributes the facing Levitical service divisions for hymns and praise to David's command; Chronicles records Solomon arranging Levitical praise and daily ministry according to that same named Davidic ordinance.

relationship: Priestly ancestry at the rebuilding's beginning
rationale: Joakim is named as son of Jesus son of Josedek, while Ezra's altar-restoration account names Iesous son of Iosedek among the priests. The different spellings are retained, and the two notices concern successive generations rather than one ceremony.
The dedication celebrates the wall whose completion is dated to the twenty-fifth of Eloul after fifty-two days; the date of completion is not automatically assigned to the later dedication ceremony.

relationship: Levitical music at renewed public worship
rationale: The dedication's Levitical songs and instruments can be compared with the Levites, instruments and accompanying trumpets at Hezekiah's restored temple worship. The wall dedication and temple offering are separate ceremonies.

relationship: Singers gather for the announced dedication; same-chapter
rationale: The singers' gathering from the surrounding district follows the request to bring Levites from their places for the wall dedication, identifying the concrete assembly purpose in the preceding notice.

The first route and the two great ones for praise are followed by the second company taking its route and both companies standing in God's house; the groups are linked by the narrative rather than made into one route.

Priests with trumpets in the dedication procession correspond to the law assigning trumpet sounding to Aaron's priestly sons and prescribing it for days of gladness and sacrifices; the law does not supply these particular musicians' identities.

The dedication uses songs of David the man of God; Hezekiah's worship reform likewise instructs the Levites to sing the Lord's praises with the words of David and Asaph. The ceremonies are not identified as one event.

relationship: David's-city steps in repair and procession
rationale: The procession ascends the steps of David's city, the same named landmark reached in the earlier wall-repair description; the adjacent pools are not equated through this link.

relationship: Broad Wall and tower landmarks revisited
rationale: The second procession passes the tower of the thennourim and reaches the Broad Wall, landmarks named in the repair notices as the Tower of the Thannourim and the Broad Wall. The differing tower-name forms are preserved.

relationship: Several repaired gates on the dedication route
rationale: The Sheep Gate, Tower of Ananeel, Fish Gate and gate of Isana occur in the earlier repair sections and again along this route. The target does not independently account for every other gate named in the procession.

relationship: Both companies reach their common destination; same-chapter
rationale: The two praise companies standing in God's house conclude the account of the first procession and the second company travelling to meet it; their distinct routes and participants are not collapsed.

The named priests sounding trumpets at the dedication perform the kind of priestly role prescribed in the law for gladness and sacrificial occasions; no identity of instruments across periods is claimed.

relationship: Public rejoicing heard at a distance
rationale: Both building-related ceremonies produce a sound heard far away. Ezra describes joy mixed with the elders' weeping at the temple foundation, while Nehemiah characterizes the wall celebration as great gladness shared by wives and children.

relationship: Treasury appointments serve the pledged provisions
rationale: The appointed custodians for first offerings, tithes and priestly and Levitical portions administer the kinds of produce and treasuries expressly included in the community's earlier pledge.

relationship: David and Solomon's service arrangements recalled
rationale: Nehemiah invokes the commandments of David and Solomon for worship duties, singers and gatekeepers; Chronicles describes Solomon implementing David's divisions for priests, Levites and gatekeepers and maintaining the royal directions for the treasuries.
The historical note that Asaph led the singers in David's days corresponds to David's appointment of Asaph as leader and his first assigning praise through Asaph and his brothers.

relationship: Levites set apart a portion for Aaron
rationale: The Levites' consecration of portions for Aaron's sons corresponds to the law requiring them to set apart a portion from received tithes and give it to Aaron. Nehemiah's unit does not itself specify the fraction.
Nehemiah expressly reports finding the Ammanite and Moabite exclusion in Moses' book; Deuteronomy states that named assembly restriction, including the forever language, in the actual source's 23:4.

relationship: The law's reasons and reversed curse
rationale: The lack of bread and water, hiring of Balaam and God's turning the curse to blessing closely follow the reasons given in Deuteronomy's assembly restriction.
Balak's complaint that he summoned Balaam to curse but received repeated blessings is a concrete narrative instance of the curse-to-blessing reversal recalled here.

relationship: Separation follows the law reading; same-chapter
rationale: The reported separation of the mixed population follows the reading of the restriction and its reasons. The broader mixed-population wording is retained, not reduced to a claim that every separated person is individually identified as Ammanite or Moabite.

The priest's closeness to Tobia can be compared with Tobia's earlier oath and marriage ties among leading Judeans; the priest's favour is not identified as either marriage named in that earlier account.

relationship: Treasury room diverted from pledged use
rationale: The room given to Tobia formerly held produce, sacred vessels and portions for worship servants, the same categories of treasury provision named in the community's pledge not to abandon God's house.
Nehemiah's absence at the king's court in Arthasastha's thirty-second year corresponds to the endpoint of the twelve-year governing period stated as the twentieth through thirty-second years.

relationship: Discovery of the earlier room arrangement; same-chapter
rationale: Nehemiah discovers the evil of the room made for Tobia, recalling the earlier notice of the priest's closeness to Tobia and preparation of that treasury chamber. The Eliasib/Elisoub forms remain as printed.

relationship: Eviction reverses the room's diversion; same-chapter
rationale: Throwing Tobia's household goods out reverses the priest's earlier provision of the large chamber for him, restoring the possibility of its sanctuary use.
The vessels, manaa and frankincense returned after purification are specifically among the room's former contents named before its diversion to Tobia.

relationship: Earlier support for worship servants fails
rationale: The unpaid Levites and singers leaving for their fields contrast with the earlier account of daily portions for singers and gatekeepers and consecrated portions for Levites; the neglected distribution has practical consequences for service.
Nehemiah's question why God's house has been abandoned directly contrasts with the community's recorded commitment that it would not abandon the house of God.

Nehemiah reports the restored delivery of wheat, wine and oil tithes to the stores. Malachi discusses retained tithes and firstfruits, then describes produce dues brought into storehouses; its unusual past-tense wording is retained rather than replaced with a familiar imperative.

The officials considered trustworthy and charged with distributing to their brothers resemble the faithful appointed administrators of firstfruits and tithes under Hezekiah; the different named personnel and reforms remain distinct.
The request that God remember kindness in His house repeats the memoir's earlier appeal to remember for good what Nehemiah had done for the people; the particular services differ.
The winepress work, loaded donkeys and burdens entering Jerusalem conflict with Jeremiah's explicit instruction to do no work and carry no burdens through the city's gates on the Sabbath.

Merchandise sold on the Sabbath to the Judeans contradicts the earlier pledge not to buy goods brought by the peoples of the land for Sabbath sale; the traders' identity is not expanded beyond this source's wording.
The rebuke for profaning the Sabbath appeals to the same requirement expressed in the command to keep it holy and do no work on the seventh day.

relationship: Warning of judgment on Jerusalem's Sabbath violation
rationale: Nehemiah connects former calamity with Sabbath profanation; Jeremiah explicitly warns that carrying burdens through Jerusalem's gates on that day will bring destructive fire on the city. This is not confused with laws about the land's sabbatical years.

relationship: Gate controls enforce the burden restriction
rationale: Closing and guarding the gates so burdens cannot be carried on the Sabbath implements the kind of restriction Jeremiah states concerning this city's gates; the precise guard schedule is Nehemiah's measure, not supplied by Jeremiah.

relationship: Outside trading meets a further warning; same-chapter
rationale: The merchants' lodging and sales outside Jerusalem are followed by Nehemiah's warning against lodging opposite the wall, after which they stop coming on the Sabbath; the account does not prohibit every later trading visit.

relationship: Warning answers the merchants' workaround; same-chapter
rationale: Nehemiah's threat responds to the preceding report of lodging and selling outside the city, and the stated result is that they no longer come on the Sabbath.

The instruction to the Levites to guard the gates and sanctify the Sabbath gives practical effect to the command to keep the day holy, without claiming that Exodus appoints these particular Levites as guards.

relationship: Foreign marriages recur as covenant concern
rationale: Both accounts describe marriages with women from surrounding peoples, including Ammanite/Ammoni and Moabite/Moabi groups. Ezra lists additional nations, while Nehemiah also names Azotian wives; the two episodes and lists are not made identical.

relationship: Earlier marriage pledge enforced by oath
rationale: The oath not to give daughters to outsiders' sons or take their daughters for the community's sons repeats the specific two-sided marriage commitment recorded in the earlier pledge.

Nehemiah uses the law's paired formula against giving daughters or taking daughters in marriage, together with its concern about turning from God. Deuteronomy's preceding context names seven Canaanite nations, while Nehemiah's immediate context names Azotians, Ammanites and Moabites; those scopes are preserved.

relationship: Solomon's foreign wives and divided heart
rationale: Nehemiah explicitly invokes Solomon as the warning example; Kings describes his foreign wives and states that they turned his heart after their gods. The supplied range has no invented 11:3 unit.
The claim that Solomon was loved by God corresponds to the birth notice explicitly saying that the Lord loved him, making his later turning aside a contrast to that favour.

Nehemiah rebukes establishing households with foreign wives as breaking faith with God; the confession in Ezra likewise calls settling foreign wives among the people covenant breaking. The speeches concern distinct stages of the community's reforms.

The marriage notice refers to a son of Joada of Elisoub, the high priest; the genealogy states that Eliasib fathered Jodae. The variant forms are retained, and the unnamed son-in-law is not assigned a name from another source.

Nehemiah prays concerning offenses against the priestly covenant and mentions the Levites; Malachi expressly addresses priests, recalls the covenant with the Levites and condemns corruption of Levi's covenant. The particular offenders and acts are not equated.

Nehemiah's assignment of priestly and Levitical service divisions according to each person's work resembles the divisions and duties set under Solomon according to David's ordinance; the later purification is not claimed as part of the earlier ceremony.

relationship: Wood and first-produce arrangements carried out
rationale: The final provision for wood carriers at intervals and the bakchouria corresponds to the pledge for scheduled wood deliveries and yearly first produce. The supplied bakchouria term is retained alongside the earlier explicit first-produce description rather than silently replaced.
